title: Understanding WCAG 2.2 (curated notes)
note: Short paraphrased explanatory notes linked to success criteria. Lower authority than the normative criterion; never overrides it.

sections.content: Text alternatives let assistive technology present non-text content to blind users, deafblind users via braille, and others. Informative images need alt text conveying purpose; decorative images should use an empty alt attribute so screen readers skip them. An img element with no alt attribute is a failure because the file name may be announced instead.

Assistive technology relies on each interface component exposing a name, role and value. A button containing only an icon, with the icon hidden from assistive technology or lacking a text alternative, has no accessible name. Fix with visible text, aria-label, aria-labelledby, or a text alternative on the icon. ARIA attributes must be spelled correctly, use allowed values, and reference IDs that exist.

Structure and relationships shown visually must also be in the markup. A visible label must be programmatically associated with its input using a label element with for/id, by wrapping the control, or via aria-labelledby. Headings should use heading elements in a logical hierarchy without skipped levels, and page regions should use landmarks such as main.

Form controls need a visible label or instructions. A text label placed near an input but not associated with it fails to give assistive technology users the same information; use a label element associated by for/id.

Links need an accessible name that describes their destination or purpose. Empty links, icon-only links without a text alternative, and vague text such as click here or read more are problems unless surrounding programmatic context clarifies the purpose.

A valid lang attribute on the html element lets screen readers choose the correct pronunciation rules and lets browsers apply language-specific features. Use a valid BCP 47 language tag such as en or fr-CA.

Contrast is computed from foreground and background colors as the relative luminance ratio. Normal text needs 4.5:1; large text needs 3:1. A contrast failure can only be asserted when the real computed colors are known.
Landmark regions such as main, nav and header let keyboard and screen reader users skip repeated content. A page should expose a main landmark.
Pointer targets should be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels unless exceptions apply. Evaluation requires rendered geometry, which static HTML does not supply.
Keyboard focus must be visibly indicated. Whether the indicator is perceivable depends on rendered styles and must be checked in a browser.
